Change the recipe and the same tool runs a completely different process. So a recipe is never edited on a whim, and changing one goes through an approved procedure.

A **Route** is the order of process steps a lot will pass through. It goes through steps such as cleaning, oxidation, exposure, etch, deposition, and measurement in turn, and because semiconductors are built layer by layer, this flow repeats many times. Which step a lot is on now is recorded by the {{term:MES|Manufacturing Execution System. A production management system that manages and records lot locations, tools, and work history in real time.}}.

### [WIP] Lots piled up in the fab

**WIP** (work in progress) is the total of lots being processed or waiting for their turn in the fab right now. As in the figure, it is the sum of lots waiting at every step. If WIP is too high, lots wait long and cycle time grows; if too low, tools have no work in front of them and sit idle.

{{toggle:Why think in lots rather than single wafers|Managing wafers one by one would mean far too many records and moves. Moving in bundles cuts movement and records, and lets you compare wafers that went through the same conditions, which makes tracing a cause easier. Lot size and how it is run do differ by company, though.}}

### [Cycle time] Most of the time is waiting

{{term:Cycle Time|The total time from a lot being released until it is complete.}} is the total time from a lot entering to coming out. With hundreds of process steps, it usually takes several weeks to several months.

{{diagram:fld-cycle|In cycle time, processing is short and waiting in front of tools is long}}

In the figure, orange is time actually being processed and gray is waiting. Waiting is far longer. A lot waits for the previous one to finish, for the tool to return from maintenance, and for the next process to free up. So shortening cycle time is mostly about **shortening the waiting.**

### [Q-time] Where waiting too long is not allowed

Not all waiting is the same. {{term:Q-time|The allowed limit on waiting time between one process and the next. Exceeding it can require rework or scrap.}} is the time allowed from the end of one process to the start of the next. It applies where the wafer changes while waiting, as a surface oxidizes again if left long after cleaning.

Exceeding the limit means rework or, in bad cases, scrap. So a lot under Q-time is treated as a **lot to process first**, and if a tool stops, it is reported at once.

> ⚠️ [Caution] Q-time limits differ by process and company. The examples in this article explain the concept; the real limit follows the work standard and the MES screen.

### [Little's law] How WIP, throughput, and cycle time relate

In a line running steadily, three values are tied by one equation.

**WIP = throughput × cycle time**

If {{term:Throughput|The amount that finishes the process and leaves per unit of time, for example the number of lots leaving per day.}} is 4 lots a day and cycle time is 4 days, WIP is 16 lots. At the same throughput, **the lower the WIP, the shorter the cycle time.** Conversely, pushing in lots without limit leaves throughput unchanged and only lengthens waiting.

### [Read next] Next article

How these terms are recorded on screen continues in the next article. Seeing how the moments a lot goes onto and comes off a tool are kept in the MES, and how tool states are divided, connects today's terms to field work. After that comes shift handover, which is also about passing the state of lots and tools to the next person accurately.

title: MES and Tool States
content:
### [Overview] Lots and tools managed in one place

In a fab where hundreds of lots move among hundreds of tools, production cannot be managed from human memory alone. So the {{term:MES|Manufacturing Execution System. A production management system that manages and records lot locations, tools, and work history in real time.}} decides "which lot to process next on which tool" and records all the results. Operators work by exchanging information with the MES through terminal screens.

{{diagram:fld-mes|MES work flow: instruction, Track-in, run, Track-out}}

| Step | What happens | What the MES keeps |
|------|--------------|--------------------|
| Instruction | Tells you the next lot and tool to process | The work target |
| Track-in | Load the lot and report the release | Start time, worker, tool |
| Run | The tool sends status and data | Process data, alarms |
| Track-out | Record completion and pass the lot to the next process | End time, result |

### [Track-in] The gate before starting

{{term:Track-in|Loading a lot on a tool and reporting the start of processing to the MES.}} is not just a start button. It is the first gate where the MES checks and permits that **this lot is the right one to be processed on this tool with this recipe.** If the lot is at a different step, the tool is in a state that is not allowed, or the recipe does not match, it will not start.

Thanks to this gate, accidents of the wrong lot going in under the wrong conditions drop. If it blocks you, do not try to bypass it. Read the message on the screen and find the cause.

> 💡 [From the field] The reason the MES refused is usually shown on the screen. If you write the message down as it is, passing it to the equipment or process engineer goes much faster.

### [Run and Track-out] While processing and after

During processing, the tool keeps sending status and process data to the MES and equipment systems. If a value drifts or an alarm occurs, it is recorded as is, and if needed the tool stops or the lot is put on hold.

When processing finishes, {{term:Track-out|Recording completion and results in the MES and passing the lot on to the next step.}} takes place. Results and process data stay in the lot history, and the MES passes the lot to the next step. Because this history exists, even if a defect appears later you can trace backward **which tool processed it, when, and under what conditions.**

{{toggle:What happens if you skip Track-in or do it wrong|The lot's location and history diverge from reality. The next person cannot find the lot, or has no history to trace the cause of a defect. So MES records are part of the work, and the actual work and the records must always match.}}

### [Tool states] A tool is always in some state

A tool is always in one of a few states, and each time the state changes it is recorded with the time.

{{diagram:fld-state|Tool states: Run, Idle, Down, PM and an example of how a day splits}}

| State | Meaning | What changes it |
|-------|---------|-----------------|
| Run | Processing a lot | Starts with Track-in, ends with Track-out |
| Idle | Able to run but no lot to process | Waiting for a lot |
| Down | Stopped by an alarm or failure | Alarm, failure, interlock |
| PM | Under planned maintenance | Starts per the maintenance schedule |

{{term:PM|Preventive Maintenance. Planned maintenance that replaces and inspects parts on a schedule before they fail.}} is a planned stop while Down is an unplanned stop. Even for the same stoppage, these two must be recorded separately to see where time is lost.

> ⚠️ [Caution] State names and how they are divided differ by company and system. This article explains the idea with four common ones; the real criteria follow your site's state definitions.

### [Why record] Uptime and improvement

As state records pile up, you can see how the 24 hours of a day were spent by state. In the figure's example, Run is 62%, Idle 20%, PM 10%, and Down 8%. From these numbers the tool's {{term:Utilization|The share of total time that a tool actually spent processing lots.}} is calculated.

Long Idle means a shortage of work or a late previous process; long Down means equipment problems must be found. An operator recording the state accurately is the starting point of improvement. If the reason for a stop is not chosen properly, the data points to the wrong place.

### [Read next] Next article

The state of tools and lots must be passed accurately to the next person at shift change. Passing on which lot is at which step, which tool is in which state, and what is not yet finished is what shift handover is about.

title: Shift Handover
content:
### [Overview] A shift change is the time that connects the work

A semiconductor fab never stops. Only the people change. So what gets passed on at shift change decides the first hour of the next shift. Information that is not passed on turns into **time the next person must spend finding out from scratch.**

{{diagram:fld-handover|Shift handover: the person handing over and the person taking over pass on four things at the tool}}

A {{term:handover|The act of the person passing the work on explaining the current state and what must be done to the person taking over, and getting it confirmed.}} is not done by word of mouth alone. Write it in the log and leave it, and talk it through at the tool while confirming. Words are forgotten, but records remain.

### [Four things] What gets passed on

| Item | What it holds | What happens if it is missing |
|------|---------------|-------------------------------|
| Tool | Running, stopped, under maintenance, anything unusual | Time is spent hunting for an abnormality already known |
| Lot | Lot number, step, hold or priority | Lots get lost or are processed in the wrong order |
| Alarm | What the alarm was and how it was handled | The same alarm comes back and you start over from zero |
| Remaining work | What to do and when | Scheduled checks or calls disappear |

> 💡 [How to read this] These four came from the question "what does the person taking over need to know to carry on right away, standing at the tool?" Formats differ by company, but the question is the same.

### [Log] So the reader can act right away

A log is **written for the reader, not the writer.** Even for the same event, how it is written makes a big difference.

{{diagram:fld-log|A vague log makes the reader ask again; a specific log lets them act at once}}

With a vague log, the person taking over must find the writer and ask again, and that person may already have gone home. A specific log contains five things.

- **When**: Write the time. Not "a while ago" but "around 14:20."
- **Where**: Write the target exactly, such as the tool name, chamber, and lot number.
- **Symptom**: Copy the alarm number and message from the screen as they are.
- **Action**: Write what you did and how it turned out.
- **What is left**: Write what the next person should continue and when.

> ⚠️ [Caution] Do not mix confirmed facts with guesses. Mark a guess as "guess" and what you verified as "confirmed." The reader will trust what is written and act on it.

{{toggle:What not to write in a log|Feelings or judgments ("this tool is always a problem," "someone must have touched it") and unconfirmed guesses written as facts. Do not use wording that blames individuals either. The log is the basis for the next person's decisions, so write it around facts and numbers.}}

### [Order] What to do at shift change

1. **Organize the log first.** Before the shift change, write all four items with nothing missing.
2. **Look together at the tool.** Pointing at the indicator lights, the screen, and the lots as you speak reduces misunderstanding.
3. **For alarms and abnormalities, say separately what is resolved and what is still to watch.**
4. **Pass on remaining work with a time.** Not "later" but "at 18:00."
5. **Get the receiver's confirmation.** Take questions, check they understood, and then sign or mark it confirmed.

> 💡 [From the field] The person taking over does not just listen. Ask on the spot about anything you do not know. A question asked at shift change costs one moment, but what goes unasked can come back as an accident.

### [Read next] Next step

With this, the three steps of getting into the field, staying safe, and reading the production flow are connected. You have seen the rules and safety to follow in the field, the language and systems in use, and how to hand work over between people. Next we move on to the basic principles behind how tools run and the basics of maintenance. From there the content gets closer to equipment theory.

title: A Guide to Semiconductor Design Roles
content:
### [Overview] What is a design job

When you turn on a smartphone, the screen changes with one tap. Behind it, billions of transistors inside a chip the size of a fingernail switch on and off in a set order. The people who **decide in advance where to put those billions and how to wire them** hold design jobs.

If field jobs in the fab make the chips that have already been decided, design jobs **draw the chip before it is made and hand it to manufacturing.** Compare it to a building: design is drawing the plans, and field work is building from them. If the plans are wrong, even perfect construction gives a building nobody can use. A chip is very hard to fix once it is made, and at advanced processes the cost of making it is large. So design is also **the work of finding what is wrong before anything is built.**

The work of design jobs falls into three threads.

- **Decide what to build**: set what the chip must do and its targets (performance, power, area, cost) and split it into blocks.
- **Draw how to build it**: write the behavior as code, place the gates, and wire them.
- **Check that it was built right**: verify in a virtual environment before building, and prepare ways to screen out defects after building.

> 💡 [How to read this] This is the first article in the design folder. Later articles cover the technical details one by one; here we only take the big picture of **who does what, which companies have these jobs, and what to prepare first.**

### [Jobs] Seven jobs share one chip

Seven kinds of jobs work on a single chip. Even on the same chip, the screen each one keeps on the monitor all day is completely different. Tap a job in the figure below to see its screen in full.

{{diagram:dsn-roles|The screens seven jobs watch all day: block diagram, code and waveforms, test status, chip floorplan, circuit waveforms, scan chain, boot log}}

**System architecture** is the starting point of design. It splits the functions customers want into blocks and sets the targets for performance, power, area, and cost. The same function can use very different amounts of power depending on the structure, so the decisions made here shape everything after.

**Digital design (RTL)** writes each block's behavior as code. Code written in {{term:RTL|Register Transfer Level. A level of description that writes, as code, how data moves between registers. It is the starting point of digital design.}} goes through a step called synthesis and becomes gates. Blocks that run on 0s and 1s, such as the CPU, memory controller, and communication interfaces, are this job's workplace.

**Design verification** checks in a virtual environment that the written code behaves as the spec says. It feeds in not only normal inputs but strange inputs and rare sequences, many times over, and raises a bug whenever the result differs from the right answer. Because a made chip is hard to fix, it is common for a large share of design staff to work on verification.

**Physical design** places the gates on the chip area and wires them. With millions to billions of gates, tools do it automatically, but it is people who set the direction so that speed, power, and area meet the targets and who clear the places where it gets stuck. The result of this stage is the layout handed to manufacturing.

**Analog design** handles continuous voltages and currents rather than 0 and 1. Typical blocks are the PLL that makes the clock, the ADC that turns signals into numbers, and the LDO that cleans up power. It is harder to automate than digital, so people spend more effort fine-tuning the circuit and layout.

**Test design (DFT)** builds test paths into the chip so defects can be found before shipping. If you cannot look inside, you cannot catch defects, so the paths are made at design time. It is the work of designing the last gate that keeps bad chips from reaching customers.

**Firmware** writes the software that runs on the chip's processor to wake and control the chip. It writes the boot code that runs first when the chip turns on, and it is often the first to check operation when the chip comes back.

> ⚠️ [Caution] Job names and boundaries differ by company and chip type. At a small company one person may do both RTL and verification; at a large one, verification itself splits into teams. When you read a job posting, read **what the job produces** rather than its name.

{{toggle:Are all seven jobs in one company|Not necessarily. A large company has all seven, but a small fabless company may solve analog or DFT with outside specialists or with IP (design blocks that already exist). Which blocks to design in-house and which to bring in is itself an important decision the architecture makes.}}

### [Timeline] Who is busy when in one project

The seven jobs do not all work at once. A chip project has five periods, and the busiest job changes with each period.

{{diagram:dsn-team|When each job is busy while making one chip: definition, design and verification, physical build, in manufacturing, chip back}}

In the first period, **definition**, the architect is busiest while the others read the targets and give opinions. In **design and verification**, RTL designers, verification engineers, and analog designers all get busy together. This period is the longest and draws the most people. In the **physical build** period, physical design leads and DFT puts in the test paths.

After the files go to manufacturing, it is the **in manufacturing** period. While the chips are being made, designers seem to catch their breath, but DFT is finishing test patterns and firmware is finishing the code to use when the chip arrives. In the last period, **chip back**, DFT and firmware are the first to switch the chip on, and if problems appear, designers and verification engineers gather again to find the cause.

One point follows. The jobs pass the baton like a relay, but **a job is not finished just because the one before it is.** If timing fails in physical design, it goes back to the RTL designer, and if the chip shows a problem, the verification engineer works again. That is why in design jobs the ability to talk with other jobs matters as much as technical skill.

### [Workplace] Which companies do design

Design jobs sit in three kinds of company, depending on how the chip gets made. The dividing line is **whether the design file goes to a fab in the same company or to a fab in another company.**

{{diagram:dsn-where|Which companies do design: fabless companies that only design, a foundry that makes chips for many customers, and IDMs that do both}}

A **fabless** company designs without a factory and outsources manufacturing to a foundry. It can focus on design without the huge investment of building a fab, and it has the largest share of design jobs. In return, it must use the process rules and parts library the foundry provides.

A **foundry** takes designs from many fabless companies and only manufactures. It has design jobs too, but they build **the tools and parts customers use**, not the customers' chips. The work is to bundle process rules, transistor models, and standard cells and give them to customers.

An **IDM** does both design and manufacturing inside one company. Design and process are close, so each can meet the other's needs right away. Designers often consult the process team, and someone who understands the process has more room to stand out in design.

> 💡 [How to read this] Even under the same name "design," the work differs a lot by company type. Checking whether the company is fabless, a foundry, or an IDM first makes a posting much easier to read.

### [Daily life] What a designer's day looks like

Unlike fab-floor jobs, design jobs spend most of the time **at a computer, running tools.** An RTL designer writes code, runs simulation, and reads waveforms. A verification engineer opens the list of failed tests from overnight in the morning and looks for the cause. A physical design engineer opens a result that a tool took hours to produce, picks out the paths where timing fails, and fixes them. This loop of **run, read the result, fix, run again** is the basic rhythm of design.

Another trait is that work stalls while tools run. A large block can take hours to a day or more per run. So designers prepare the next task while waiting, and they build the habit of planning so that **each run checks as much as possible.**

Meetings are a big part of the job too. The architect, designers, verification, and physical design meet regularly to share progress and what is stuck, and when the spec changes they tell the affected jobs right away. Being good at writing code matters, but so does **organizing your work so that the next person can pick it up**; that is also a skill in design.

{{toggle:Is design just good coding|Only partly. RTL is written as code, but it describes how hardware works, so it does not run line by line like software. You need practice writing while imagining a circuit in which every statement exists at the same time. Verification and firmware are closer to software development, while analog and physical design depend more on understanding devices and wiring.}}

### [Connection] Where design meets the fab

Design and the fab may look like separate worlds, but they **meet in three places.** The first is design rules. The process has a finest line width and spacing it can make reliably, and the design must keep to them. Break the rules and the chip cannot be made or defects rise. The second is yield. Even with the same process, packing wires tightly or using weak shapes increases defects, so designers sometimes choose shapes that raise yield. The third is test. To screen the chips that come out of the fab, you need the test paths put in at design time.

That is why someone who knows the process can stand out in design, and someone who knows design can narrow down the cause of defects faster in the fab. People who understand both worlds are rare, so their value is high. Later in this folder we cover these meeting points on their own (design rules and DFM, and how design affects yield).

### [Preparation] What to prepare first

The basic subjects you learn in school are used differently by each job. In the figure below, tap a job to see which subjects matter for it.

{{diagram:dsn-skills|Basic subjects used by each job: the number in each circle is how many jobs use that subject}}

The subjects that reach the most jobs are **digital logic**, **coding**, and **computer architecture.** Whatever the job, these become the common vocabulary. For analog, circuit theory and semiconductor devices are central, and in physical design and DFT, people who understand the process stand out. The numbers count common tendencies and differ by company and team.

Where you start also depends on your major. Electronics, electrical, and computer majors tend to lead into digital design, verification, and analog. Materials, chemistry, and physics majors can find strength **where process and design meet** (design rules, yield, device models). Either way, there are things you can try first.

- **Review digital logic**: combinational and sequential circuits, and the idea of a clock
- **Try one design language**: write a few simple circuits yourself in Verilog or SystemVerilog
- **Learn the big picture**: the order from spec to manufacturing (the next article, "Chip Design Flow")
- **Learn the vocabulary**: RTL, Netlist, GDS, PPA (the article after that, "Design Terms")

### [Postings] How to read a job posting

Design postings can look alike by name, but there is a way to read them. First, look at **what the job produces.** "RTL design" produces code, "verification" a test environment, and "physical design" a layout. Next, look at **which tools and languages** it uses. Names like Verilog, SystemVerilog, SPICE, and scripting languages are clues to what the job really does. Finally, look at **which chip and which stage.** Even physical design looks quite different for a mobile chip, a memory, and an analog chip. With these three, you can tell apart postings that share a name but differ in the work.

### [Summary] What to take away from this article

- A design job is the work of **drawing the chip before it is made and finding what is wrong.**
- **Seven jobs** work on one chip, and each sees a different screen and asks different questions.
- The busiest job changes with each period of a project, and **communication between jobs** matters as much as skill.
- Design sits in three kinds of company, **fabless, foundry, and IDM**, and the work looks different in each.
- Digital logic, coding, and computer architecture are the **common foundation** of many jobs.

The rest of the articles in this folder are arranged to be read from the front of the flow to the back. In the next article we follow the nine steps from an idea to a chip.

title: Chip Design Flow
content:
### [Overview] In what order is a chip made

Chip design is **the process of turning a request in words into an increasingly concrete form.** At first it is a single line like "a fast, low-power chip for a smartphone"; then it becomes a block structure, then code, then a connection of gates, and finally shapes on silicon. We split this flow into nine steps.

{{diagram:dsn-flow|Nine steps from an idea to a chip}}

| Step | What happens | What it hands over |
|------|--------------|--------------------|
| 1. Spec | Write down what the chip must do and its targets | Requirements document |
| 2. Architecture | Split into blocks and decide how they connect | Block structure |
| 3. RTL design | Write each block's behavior as code | RTL code |
| 4. Verification | Check that the code behaves as the spec says | Test results, bug list |
| 5. Synthesis | Turn the code into a connection of gates | Netlist |
| 6. Physical design | Place the gates and wire them up | Placement and routing result |
| 7. Sign-off | Do the final check before manufacturing | Pass confirmation |
| 8. Tape-out | Send the final layout file to the manufacturer | GDS file |
| 9. Manufacturing and test | Make the chips and screen out defects | Real chips |

> 💡 [How to read this] The flow looks one-way, but in practice **you often go back.** A bug found in verification sends you back to RTL; a timing miss in physical design sends you back to synthesis or RTL. This article is a map for walking the road once.

### [Front] From definition to verification

The first four steps **define and check the chip's behavior.** The spec and architecture decide what the chip must do and how to split it into blocks. The performance, power, and area targets set here guide every later step. If the targets are vague, even excellent work later heads in the wrong direction.

RTL design and verification keep cycling. The designer writes a block, the verification engineer runs it in a virtual environment, and when a bug shows up the designer fixes it and verifies again. The two **repeat every time the code changes.**

### [Back] From synthesis to manufacturing

The last five steps **turn behavior into physical form.** {{term:Synthesis|The process of turning RTL code into a connection of real gates (logic elements). A synthesis tool does it automatically, aiming at the speed targets in the constraint file (SDC).}} lets a tool read the code and convert it to gates. Physical design places those gates on the chip area and wires them. Sign-off is the last check of timing, power, and design rules, and once everything passes comes {{term:tape-out|Sending the finished final layout file (GDS) to the manufacturer. After this, fixing anything is very hard.}}. The name comes from the old days when the file was sent on magnetic tape.

When manufacturing ends and chips come back, test equipment screens out defects chip by chip. The design team checks real operation on a real chip for the first time, and if something is wrong they hunt for the cause. This stage is **post-silicon validation.**

### [Cost] Why try to find bugs early

The cost of fixing a bug differs greatly depending on when in the flow you find it.

{{diagram:dsn-loop|The later a bug is found, the more it costs: from verification to after the chip exists}}

If you find it during verification, you fix one line of code and rerun the test. If you find it after physical design is done, you must redo synthesis and placement and routing. If you find it after the chip is made, you must redo masks and manufacturing, and the schedule can slip by months. The multipliers in the figure are only for building a feel; real costs differ by company and chip.

{{toggle:This is why verification gets so much time|Once a chip is made it is very hard and costly to fix. So the most time and people go to finding bugs in a virtual environment before building. A bug that verification misses becomes more expensive the later it appears, so verification is less "done" and more "I can't find any more."}}

### [Files] The file handed over at each step

Each step of the flow **makes a file and hands it to the next.** Knowing the file's name tells you where in the flow you are.

{{diagram:dsn-handoff|The file handed over at each step: spec, RTL, netlist, GDS, test patterns}}

The spec is writing, RTL is code, the netlist is a connection of gates, and GDS is shapes. The further along, the harder for people to read and the easier for tools. The next article, "Design Terms," goes through these files one by one.

> ⚠️ [Caution] Step names and how they are split differ a little by company. For example, one team may do both synthesis and physical design, or sign-off may be counted as part of physical design. This article uses the most common nine steps.

title: Design Terms (RTL · Netlist · GDS · PPA)
content:
### [Overview] Design terms are names for conversions

Design talk keeps using words like RTL, netlist, GDS, and PPA. Rather than memorize them one by one, it is easier to see them as **names for the order in which a chip takes a more concrete form.** Even a single adder starts as "add two numbers," then becomes code, then gates, and finally shapes.

{{diagram:dsn-abs|One adder at four levels: behavior, RTL, netlist, GDS}}

Going from top to bottom, **more things are decided.** At the behavior level it is not yet decided what circuit to build; at RTL the registers and the calculation are decided; at the netlist the actual gates are decided; at GDS even the positions of the shapes are decided. This way of dividing into levels is called {{term:abstraction level|The degree of detail with which the same circuit is viewed. The higher the level, the simpler; the lower, the more detailed.}}.

### [Files] RTL, netlist, GDS

The three main files a design passes through are these.

| Term | One-line meaning | Who makes it |
|------|------------------|--------------|
| RTL | Behavior written as code | Digital designer |
| Netlist | A list of gates and their connections | Synthesis tool |
| GDS | The shape file of the chip layout | Physical design tools and engineers |

**RTL** stands for Register Transfer Level, a level that writes as code how data moves between registers. It is the highest-level file that designers write by hand. The **netlist** is the list of gate connections a synthesis tool produces from RTL. From this stage on, speed and area can be measured as numbers. **GDS** is a file format that holds the chip layout, and this file is the input for making masks. Handing it to manufacturing is tape-out.

> 💡 [How to read this] "RTL is out," "we got the netlist," and "GDS is handed over" each say **where in the flow we are now.** If you catch only these three words in a meeting, you can see the progress.

### [Conversion] Words that help the conversions

A few agreements and checks go along with the moves between the three files.

{{diagram:dsn-terms|A map of common design terms: RTL, netlist, GDS with SDC, PDK, STA and DRC}}

{{term:SDC|Synopsys Design Constraints. A constraint file that states the speed targets to meet, such as the clock period and input and output timing. Both synthesis and timing checks read this file.}} is a constraint file that states speed targets. Tools choose and place gates to meet these targets. {{term:PDK|Process Design Kit. A bundle of process documents that a foundry gives designers. It contains transistor models, design rules, and standard cell libraries.}} is the bundle of process documents the foundry provides. A design can only be built from the parts and rules in this bundle. STA and DRC are names of checks. STA checks that every path arrives in time, and DRC checks that shapes obey the process rules.

{{toggle:What is a standard cell|It is a ready-made collection of parts that a synthesis tool uses when it picks gates. Basic gates such as AND, OR, and flip-flops are prepared in different sizes and speeds, and a foundry or library company provides them as part of the PDK. Designers do not draw gates from scratch; they take these cells, which is why they are called "standard."}}

### [Goals] The three goals called PPA

Design always weighs three things at once.

{{diagram:dsn-ppa|PPA: the balance of Performance, Power, and Area}}

**Performance** is how fast the chip works, **power** is how much it uses, and **area** is how big the chip is. Their initials give PPA. Raising speed tends to raise power and area together, and cutting power tends to slow the chip down. Cutting area lets more chips come from one wafer and lowers cost, but leaves less speed margin. So a design goal is set by "which of the PPA comes first." Server chips lean toward speed, battery devices toward power, and price-sensitive chips toward area.

> ⚠️ [Caution] The three in PPA are not independent. If someone says only one is good, ask how the others look. When an interviewer asks "is this design good," it is safer to first say **by what standard** it is good.

If you know these four terms (RTL, netlist, GDS, PPA), you can follow half of any design conversation. From the next article on, we look at each step in depth.
